I'm a smaller woman, and found the grip on my Canon 30D to be uncomfortable, but I wasn't willing to compromise on photo quality so a digicam was out. When I discovered micro four thirds cameras, I tried out the Oly E-P1 and E-LP1, but preferred the feel of the GF1. I also tried out the Samsung NX10, but it just doesn't offer enough native lenses for me.

The GF1 is the most comfortable camera I've ever owned. The image quality is very good, and although I hear it's good on full auto, I use mine on full manual or shutter priority, and it's very easy to use if you've had any experience with a full featured camera. The buttons and menus are very intuitive, the wheel at the top of the camera is easy to use and I like the flash to use as a fill flash. At default I got a few blown highlights, but this is very easy to control by stepping down just a little.

The only things that I didn't love are the rear dial - it's a little more recessed than I'd like, although I got used to it pretty quickly - and I would have preferred a flip and twist screen since the camera doesn't come with a view finder. Otherwise I'm very satisfied with this camera.

The 14-45mm kit lens is good quality. It's solid with no rattles, turns with just enough resistance, and takes sharp high quality pics with very little chromatic aberration.

One thing last worth mentioning is the stabilization. It's in the lens, and it works better than I expected. I got handheld pics reliably at speeds I haven't been able to shoot at before. That being said, if you prefer your stabilization in the camera rather than in the lens, the E-PL1 is definitely worth checking out.

I'm very happy with the GF1, particularly the easy menus and controls. It takes the annoyances out of photography so I can concentrate on taking the pics rather than fighting the camera. With good image quality, nice videos, fast auto focus and better than average auto features, this seems like a camera for anyone interested photography, from newbie to pros looking for a smaller second camera. For enthusiasts like me, it's just the ticket!

Note: I would love to love this speaker set, but it has inconsistent performance with various devices. I received a review sample and was pleased by the sound when I plugged this into the phone port on my ThinkPad T61. The sound was clear and I could hear every note on the album that I use to test speakers (Miles Davis' [[ASIN:B000002ADT Kind of Blue]]). I use that album because the instruments in the ensemble cover low, mid and high range frequencies. The bass was a little thin, but with the speakers less than two feet away the sound was rich and I was happy.

Where I started to experience problems was when I plugged this into the 3.5mm port on my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 phone. There was static in the mix. The same with my [[ASIN:B00D029NNA Samsung Galaxy Tab 3 10.1 inch]] - static interfered with the music. My final test was to plug the 3.5mm cable end into an [[ASIN:B00AEJJRBK Avantree Cara Bluetooth 4.0 Handsfree stereo Car Kit with mic]] and connect via bluetooth. The sound was crystal clear.

I am not sure what conclusions to draw. It could be something wrong with the Samsung phone and tablet, although both work perfectly with headphones which I have directly plugged into their 3.5mm ports. It may be that the 3.5mm cable and interface on the input of this speaker is overly sensitive to impedance and the slightest deviation will induce static. I am not sure, but because I was unable to get the same quality consistently across all devices with which I tested these speakers I subtracted two stars.

Construction is exceptional, although I wish the design employed removable USB and 3.5mm cables instead of the fixed ones that provide power and signal inputs, and connect the two units. As it stands if a cable breaks it will take some skill to repair it. With removable, off-the-shelf cables a broken one can be rectified with a trip to an electronics store.

Overall, on the two devices that I tested with which these speakers worked the sound was spectacular. On the other two it was unlistenable. If you are connecting this to a bluetooth receiver it's probably a safe choice, but if you are connecting this to anything else I would proceed with caution.

Smart watches have gotten more popular with the release of the Apple watch. They tend to have a standard set of functions, such as access to instant messaging, email, time, alarms and a lot more, typically tied to your phone. Not all smart watches are alike, though, and offer different sets of functions, better connectivity and other various differences from one another. This particular smart watch offers the mainline set of functions, setting itself apart through the user interface which is more polished and clean than most others with which I have worked. That said, I have a couple of quibbles with it, leaving room for a little improvement.

This is a standard-sized watch with a rubber wristband that can actually fit a larger wrist like mine. I have trouble finding watches and watch bands that fit me, so the fact that this one fits me is a pleasant surprise.

Powering it on, the user is immediately greeted with a complex and fairly complete visual menu system with tiles for every function available to the user. This is a standard presentation for a smartwatch, but this one looks a bit more polished and clean than the others I have seen. Switching to other menu screens just requires a swipe gesture, as to be expected. I have big hands, and this means that, for me, using a stylus makes working with this watch a lot easier. This is not the fault of the watch but a reality of working with a small device.

My first issue with this watch came when I paired it to my phone. The date and time on the watch were off, so I expected that it would grab the time from my iPhone when I paired it. It did not. Instead, I had to dig for the clock application and manually set the time. I dislike this and think that having it set itself when it is paired is much more accurate and cuts effort on the part of the user. For Android users, there is an application to allow for syncing up the time, date and more, but iOS users are out of luck for now. To the manufacturer's credit this is made clear on the product listing so this is not a surprise. Regardless, I am of the opinion that the watch should fetch the time, not rely on being sent the time. In the grand scheme of things, though, this is an annoyance, not a deal breaker.

There is a fairly comprehensive list of functions provided by this watch in addition to time/date and phone answer. Through the menus the user has access to call logs and function, Bluetooth functions, a remote finder function, a pedometer, a sleep monitor, a reminder function to get up and move on occasion, calendar and clock functions, audio functions, video functions and a few more.

One of the interesting functions that this watch offers is a camera. So, I tried to use it and it complained that there was no memory card available. Reading through the limited documentation included, I was unable to find anything about a memory card. I finally noticed that the back of the watch has a small groove where it can be popped off, and when I removed the back I found the battery which is removable (replaceable - another pleasant surprise). Under the battery is a slot for a micro SD card.

Adding a memory card comes with a big catch. It requires removing the battery to get at the holder which in turn clears the clock and resets it to midnight 01-01-2015. So, adding the memory card requires me to set the time again. And again if I remove the card.

Although I think the time sync functions of this watch are lacking, it is otherwise a good smartwatch. The interface is professional and polished and the whole provides access to a large number of useful functions. It's priced well too. Overall, this is a solid offering worth a look if you are wanting a smartwatch.

I'm not a fan of the ultra-thin profiles of most tablets. Understandably if its a smart phone you want it to slip into a pocket easily but with a tablet for home use there isn't much occasion where it needs to be ultra-slim and consequently unwieldy and as secure as a wet bar of soap. That being said, I know these are meant to be travel friendly and as such I'm glad that they are small and sleek and, in the case of the Lenovo M8 HD, power misers as well. I'm okay with this because I occasionally travel with my tablet and because the remedy for the non-tactile properties of the ultra-sleek tablet is a silicone case like this one. They're not expensive, they do a darned good job of protecting the tablet, and they make the tablet much easier to handle in and around the house.

Normally I don't look for a feature rich version of the silicone case. It's usually going to be just a simple stretch into place "skin" of sorts where corners are protected and screen is recessed to where it is protected from drops and such. Those usually hover around the $10 mark or so. What intrigued me about this case was the rotating stand and the handstrap feature. I use the tablet in bed often as it sits on my nightstand. I also occasionally use it in the kitchen or bathroom too. So those features would undoubtedly come in handy. My first thought was that paying double the cost was a little out of form but that was followed by, "what's another $10?"

The case installs in parts that are intuitive and easy to fit. Some stretching is required and some massaging of corners to get everything to fit. But once in place everything fits perfectly. Buttons work great and have good feel, the power jack is covered by a silicone flap which is easy to access as needed. Cameras front and back show fine and the speaker is exposed. The case itself is nice and hefty, easy to carry, non-slip in enough areas, and dare I say "bouncy" in all the right places.

I removed the shoulder strap retainers that came pre-installed as I don't see myself carrying the case that way. I put those away with the shoulder strap as a just-in-case item for later. The handstrap adjusted with velcro easily and the stand works great. The fact that the stand/strap mount rotates 360 degrees is awesome as it adapts to whatever angle your hand is at whatever orientation that you're standing the tablet on any flat surface. This was of instant benefit as I slipped my hand in and it felt both comfortable and secure.

The one feature I do wish it had was covers for the cameras. I ended up 3D printing some covers for it. I also feel like there is little to no bezel clearance for a tempered glass screen protector although the case itself has enough flex to accommodate it anyway so I'll be adding one in the near future. That being said the case provides a substantial amount of protection for the screen as long as it gets dropped on a flat surface. Conclusion: Well worth the money as it is grippy, wieldy, standy, grabby, and functionally perfect.

First and foremost let's get to the issue of PU leather, check Google or Wikipedia, it's not leather. It looks like leather. It feels somewhat like leather and it's supposed to be easier to clean than real leather. To me there's not really a lot of difference. The brown cover is handsome and reminds me quite a lot of old leather bound novels. The color is just awesome. The fit is as good, maybe better, than my Amazon PaperWhite specific cover. I usually put my name, phone and email contacts under my Kindles. I couldn't get this OFF of my Kindle! I have bruises on several finger tips from trying. I may have to use a screw driver to carefully pry this off or I may need to cut this off if I decide to go back to my custom air-brushed Amazon cover. I'm going to leave it on for now. I've had black Kindle covers for years. This does everything the Amazon case does. There's decent protection for the Kindle. It has a magnetic clasp that automatically turns the Kindle on and off. It certainly holds the Kindle well enough. The cover folds back all the way for easy one handed reading. I'd have given it five stars but for one thing, the company thought it was a good idea to emboss their company name on the front cover. I just don't care for that. It's small so no one's going to see it. The only person who will see the embossed name is me and I've already got the product. I don't need to be constantly reminded who made it.

{Edit - 06/13/16}
Just slightly more than a year since I obtained this case. I've left it on all this time because I really do like the brown color and the lack of the metal plate the Amazon case comes with. Fit's been perfect only had a couple issues where opening didn't turn the Paperwhite on but even the Amazon brand has that issue from time to time. My biggest problem is all the brown on the edges and corners either is or has already fallen off. The bulge where the magnet sits is beginning to split open. It's gotten some hard use and been with me in my walker bag for this past year but it hasn't worn well and while I still like the color I'm not sure I want to replace this with the same brand if, even at this price, it only lasts a year before falling apart. Makes me sad. Dropped from four to three stars.

2nd Edit June 17th 2016 -
Inateck responded quickly to my review edited and comments about their product falling apart. I'm very impressed by their customer service which got the new cover to me very quickly even though I could find no warranty information for the product anywhere. They even allowed me to make a color change and select the red instead of the brown I had originally had. I hope this cover lasts longer than a year. Thank you for standing behind your product.

I recently purchased a new zoom lens for my camera after I broke the old one when I took a tumble. I had filters like these for my old lens but the thread size was different so my old filters were no longer useful. I selected this filter for my new lens, somewhat apprehensively because of the relatively low asking price. It has proven to be a decent filter but it is not useful in all situations.

The idea behind this filter is light diffusion which will give an image a very slight haze or softness, depending on the lighting and subject. This is an effect that can be emulated in software during post-processing but in doing this type of enhancement I have found it is sometimes unnatural. It certainly is less fun than making it happen while shooting, which is why these types of filters are available.

In use it works, though I have had mixed results. When using it with certain light sources, the filter seems to have no real effect at all, while with others it creates a subtle, soft glow around the subject. I am still working out the situations where it is most effective. I have had similar issues with filters like these with other lenses, and as such I assume the problem is in my lack of practice with them. It will take some time and practice to make my results more consistent, and for now I lay the fault on myself.

The build quality seems to be good. I have received filters in the past where the glass rattles in the frame which is unsettling. This one is tight and there is no play between the glass and the frame. It screws on to the lens securely and is easy to clean.

The asking price is quite reasonable. I have seen these filters priced much higher, and I have also seen much cheaper ones that do not work well. The pricing seems in line with the product, if not slightly low.

I have no complaints with this filter. The issues I have with it are probably my inexperience, and I will keep working with it to improve my results. I will return here and update my review if my impression changes. For now, though, I am satisfied.

I purchased this for two specific reasons: (1) safety because too many accidents are caused by drivers with a phone to their ear, and (2) I love music and my Droid X has become my MP3 player (among other things as well as a phone.

This device comes with a fairly short USB charging cable that connects to a port on the head. The length made it inconvenient, and it was pretty flimsy too, failing after about three months. I added a [[ASIN:B0042X8XQO PowerLine 90310 Auto Socket Splitter with USB Power Port]] (which cleared my console in my 2008 Mazda 3 with the GOgroove and [[ASIN:B000S5Q9CA Motorola Vehicle Power Adapter micro-USB Rapid Rate Charger]] plugged in), and the combination, while unwieldy, has worked perfectly ever since.

Music and calls are reasonably clear. I do have to turn my radio volume up when a call comes in, but that may be an issue with my phone and not the GOgroove. And, like a hands-free system should work, when there is an incoming call or you wish to make an outgoing one, the MP3 player feature in my Droid X pauses the music until I am finished using the phone. After calls are terminated any paused music will automatically resume.

For long trips where you pass through areas with radio stations, your clear signal set in one location may start to degrade and you will notice static. That is caused by you coming into the range of a strong FM signal that is competing with the one you selected. You will need to seek and switch to a new frequency when that happens. For example, if I am traveling from, say, Ormond Beach, FL to Jacksonville, FL, I will need to change my frequency twice going up and twice again returning. It's the nature of any such device and there is nothing that can be designed into the GOgroove to fix it - at least not at the price point at which this device is selling.

I've had friends connect to it with their iPhones, and it works without a hitch. The icing on the cake is the GOgroove remains paired with my Droid X, and automatically connects to it as soon as I start my car if I am playing music. This is a convenient feature that I wish my [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]] that is connected to my home stereo had - I have to manually connect to that device anytime I want to use it.

Overall I am thrilled with my GOgroove and if it dies I would not hesitate to purchase another. In fact, I am considering purchasing a spare anyway because I spend a lot of time in my car and life without this wonderful gizmo would not be the same.

I ordered this lens and filter kit to go with my Samsung NX300 with the intent of expanding the capabilities of the camera without spending a fortune. I looked at several different kits before settling on this one, based on the price. I will admit to being a bit apprehensive about the cost in relation to the number of lenses and filters in the kit (presently this kit sells for less than $35 on Amazon as I write this) but my concern was ill-placed - this is a good kit.

I will start off by saying that I am not a professional photographer by any stretch of the imagination. I could be best described as an enthusiast who is trying to learn as I go.

I have experimented and played with many of the various components with this kit, starting with the 2.2x telephoto lens. This is a chunky item, which should be expected as it is a glass lens. It attached without issue to my 18mm-55mm OIS lens and I was able to use it almost immediately out of the box. It took me a little fiddling at first to get the focus just right as I am still learning with the camera but once I figured out the manual focus I was able to improve the zoom range with the telephoto lens in place. This, to me, is worth the cost of the kit. One thing I did notice, however, is that when the telescoping zoom is not fully extended on the regular lens, this lens adds a shadowy blackout area around the perimeter of the image that fades when the zoom is telescoped out.

My favorite component of this kit is the .43x wide-angle lens which works surprisingly well with the camera's included lens. It is another chunky item like the telephoto lens and it attaches easily as well. Even at closer ranges (15 feet or so) it allows the camera to capture appreciably more than the regular lens, without distortion. This is probably the one component I will use more than the others, and again this is an accessory that is worth the cost of the kit. This lens is not going to give the same quality result as a dedicated wide-angle lens but the price/quality tradeoff is worth it.

There are four close-up lenses in this kit that vary in strength. These are fun to play with though I did start to get a lot of edge distortion when using the strongest lens. This is not a problem as there are times when this kind of distortion is a good thing. I was able to get similar close-up shots - without distortion - with the Samsung lens but it required a lot more effort. Interestingly, one of these lenses had a smudge on it when I removed it from it's cellophane envelope. A quick wipe with a microfiber cloth did a fine job of cleaning the lens but this puzzled me - why was it smudged?

The wide-angle lens comes coupled with a macro lens that is absolutely astounding for close-up shots. I use this lens for taking pictures of pattern weaves, close-ups of surfaces, animal fur and other interesting subjects (the knee of my denim jeans makes a really interesting background shot). It works even a little better than the close-up lenses and is likely going to be the only lens I use for when I need a really detailed close-in shot of something. Though this lens outperforms the close-up magnifying lenses it requires decoupling from the wide-angle lens before it can be used and this is a minor hassle.

The kit includes a UV filter, a CPL filter and a FL-D filter. I used the CPL filter while experimenting and the result was minorly disappointing but I figured that was due to unrealistic expectations. It did tweak the color profile just a little but not dramatically like I had hoped. The FL-D filter was another story and gave the whole picture a completely different color profile. It is designed for use with fluorescent lighting (which means it should be used a lot when indoors) so when it is used with incandescent lighting it give a very eerie and unusual hue to pictures. With my lens I can adjust for fluorescent lighting electronically so this isn't a lens I necessarily need but I still like to mess with it. I have not tried the UV filter.

The cleaning kit is an important item in the kit, for removing dirt and smudges from the various lenses without using a harsh cloth. It's very basic but is a fine start - cleaning spray, cotton swabs, a microfiber cloth and a squeeze duster for puffing away particles when a full cleaning is not needed.

This kit includes a couple of other miscellaneous items as well, including a miniature tripod for a desk mount and a 6-compartment memory card storage case. These are nice-to-have extras, though I confess I am thoroughly unimpressed with the tripod which is a flexible bendy-leg tripod that does not retain the position in which it is set when supporting the camera, so it really is of little use. I continue to mess with the tripod, though, as I am sure I can get it to work in certain scenarios.

The main negative I encountered so far was actually the manner in which the kit was packaged and shipped to me. Everything was in a large plastic envelope bag with no padding at all. What would prevent the items in the kit from being crushed in such a shipment? Fortunately, all items were individually wrapped in small and sturdy cardboard boxes and one of those boxes was actually slightly crushed though there was no damage to the merchandise inside. Something like this should be shipped in a larger corrugated box, to better protect everything.

If you have a Samsung camera for which this kit is compatible, this is a very good kit to extend the capability of the camera without breaking the bank. The various lenses add range and effects, the filters are nice to have on hand and the extras are icing on the cake. At the current pricing, this is a very good deal.

Even though I have always had an interest in astronomy I was never able to work a course in this subject in my college schedule or afterwards. When I saw this telescope offered I realized that now I had both the time and the means to explore my interest a bit further. I had very little difficulty setting the scope up, and spent some time familiarizing myself with the various components. I practiced using this by checking out objects in my neighborhood, and managed to get an 'up close and personal' view of some birds in a neighbor's yard and quickly realized that this scope was powerful.

That evening I took the scope to an upstairs window to see what I could see, and despite the pesky street light was able to get a great view of the full moon (btw did you know that it sparkles a bit?). I saw details that I had only seen in photos before which was fascinating. Then I decided to take a look at Mars, which was near the Moon that evening. That is when things got complicated. The finder scope and the main scope need to be synced, and I don't know how to do this (yet). With some fiddling, and aided by Mars' close proximity to the Moon I was able to find Mars, which was exciting but for some reason it was distorted (it had a starburst appearance). My husband and I fiddled with various lenses and combinations to try to eliminate this but were unsuccessful. The experimentation was further complicated by the touchiness of the stand....it was difficult to make small, smooth adjustments and to keep the scope locked in position. Some of this is no doubt due to our in expertise, some I think is due to the equipment.

My enjoyment of this scope would have been much greater if more instructions had been provided. We discovered, more or less by accident how to lock, at least partially, the scope into place. We managed to make some focusing adjustments by trial and error. Even some rudimentary instructions in a small booklet or even a sheet or two describing how to adjust, focus and lock the scope as well as an illustration of the scope with all the components clearly labeled with a brief description of their function would have been greatly appreciated. This is a basic instrument, one that will primarily be used by beginners or novices who will not necessarily be familiar with this equipment. Basic instructions should have been included. As it is my unfamiliarity with the various aspects of the telescope make following many of the instructions I do find on-line difficult to follow.

Despite this problems I am enjoying my new toy. I found the stand to be steady, and the tray located on the stand to be a handy place to put lenses and covers. As I mentioned earlier this is a surprisingly (at least to this beginning user) powerful scope. I'm going to play around with this some more, and will probably upgrade some of the lenses and add some accessories based on my experiences. Besides star gazing I think this will be a great item to watch birds or wild life, and it is certainly portable and forgiving enough to take on a camping trip.

After a bad experience with another flat amp antenna I purchased the leaf for just over $50 .
It picks up 19 stations in the "low country" around a lot of tall pine trees.(20 is the max number of stations in a 60 mile radius here with any antenna according to the TV manufacturer).

You can paint the ant/ cables to match the walls. Comes with push pins for walls and Velcro for wall or window if you want them.Also has a plug into TV for the amp or you can plug into the wall like I did so it isn't hampered by the surge protector.

I get ABC, CBS,NBC,FOX,THIS,3 PBS stations, 3 Christian channels,a Spanish channel, WE,GET,MY,BOUNCE,YOU TOO, one music video channel and one other. The reception on all (but 2) is exceptionally strong with no blips in power even if you cannot put it in a window. I have mine hanging behind my curtain and most channels get 90-100% station strength almost constantly when 35%, even 30% will give you the station clear enough to watch a program with very few "blips" in reception.

I am enjoying not adjusting the Rabbit ear antenna (when I watched certain channels) even though it worked *good* enough for the money.

If you had another antenna before that only picked up 5-13 channels (for exp.) and you switch to a more powerful one like this, remember to unplug your TV a good minute before re- auto programming ( I forgot at first myself) as some TVs seem to "remember" how many it gets and stops at that number.

The Logitech Folio Touch is a JOY to type on. I really love typing on it — I’m writing this review using the case. I’ve typed quite a few long documents on it. I turn to this keyboard when I want distraction-free writing.

I downloaded the Logitech Control app, but it doesn’t seem to give any options for customizing the keyboard. All I see the app do is check for keyboard firmware updates. When I wanted to change the trackpad scrolling direction, I had to hunt through the iPad’s settings — I thought that would be in the Logitech app. (I learned those settings became part of iOS, so the Logitech app seems … unnecessary.)

I don’t really like the trackpad. I’ve used Logitech mice for years. My current daily mouse is the Logitech MX Master 3, so I *know* they can do a good Mac mouse. But I just feel like they dropped the ball with this trackpad. The trackpad works but it could be better. I notice drag at times, and I don’t like the noise or tactile feedback when I click it. I can adjust a few settings (scrolling direction, tracking speed, tap to click, and two finger secondary click) in the iPad’s General Settings, but I want to be able to customize more through Logitech.

The corners of the case are reinforced. The bumper is a bit thick, too thick for some hubs or USB-C cables to fit without using an extension cable. There is a cutout for the power button so Touch ID can be used. There’s a spot for the Apple Pencil, it can rest inside the bumper or fit through a slot on the latch.

The Folio Touch pairs via the Smart Connector, so it’s super easy to set up: just stick your iPad inside and it’s ready to go. The iPad powers the keyboard, so I don’t have to remember to charge it, which I like. I haven’t noticed it being a battery hog.

Overall, I really like the Logitech Folio Touch. I actually use my iPad more now, since I like typing on the keyboard so much. The case has made my iPad more functional for me.

I'm a big fan of the 8x32 style of binoculars. These aren't as bright or powerful as the 10x42 or 8x42 binoculars on the market, but they are 1/3 to 1/2 less bulky and lighter weight. Realistically, the larger 42mm binoculars are mostly brighter than the 32mm size at dawn and dusk, which is not when I'm hiking. 8x vs 10x is a personal preference, but a lot of people prefer 8x because the image is easier to hand-hold (in addition to the smaller size and lower weight).

Celestron makes a wide variety of binoculars, including a lot of basic-quality entry-level stuff that is not built very well and doesn't perform very well. This TrailSeeker ED model is a big step up from entry-level, both in price and performance. This model isn't quite as good as the top-rated 8x32 models like Nikon Monarch or Zeiss Terra, which both sell for around $400, but I think it is at least as good as any of the competition selling for under $300 that I have tried. I see a bright clear image with no noticeable chromatic aberration. Field of view is much better than most 8x32 binoculars and the image is sharp over a wider area than other under-$300 binoculars that I have tried. Field of view is very useful if your subject moves quickly or unpredictably (birds, wild mammals, sports athletes, etc). Build quality has been very solid and reliable for me so far.

Some people complain that the Celestron warranty is not as good as the competition and this is true. Some of the other brands have a "no questions asked" return policy for a good period time. Celestron's warranty is very limited in comparison, so definitely take that into consideration, especially if you are hard on your equipment.

This is a good basic router for a single user who primarily streams YouTube or Netflix to one laptop at a time. My wife loves birdwatching and our teenage son enjoys stargazing so we have an assortment of binoculars and inexpensive telescopes. Before this monocular I had never used one and even though I have not had it very long at all I am already very pleased with it. Though it is ideal for bird watching and field work, it also will work as an amateur telescope.

At roughly 7" long, this monocular is large enough to be usable but small enough to fit in a coat pocket or even in a briefcase. It comes in a nice, nylon-weave carrying pouch that even has a belt loop so carrying it into the field is easy and does not take up extra room. It also has a holding strap much like a camcorder does so it can be held more securely. It has a small metal tripod suitable for setting up on a desk or table. It’s not a big tripod - the legs extend to 7.5" - but is works well if you are recording or are seated and need a steady hand. Finally, it includes a microfiber cleaning cloth in the box for wiping the lenses safely without scratching them.

This is a waterproof monocular and everything about it showcases that. There are two rubberized caps for either end that cover the lenses and keep out moisture and dust when not in use. These are physically attached to the barrel (one by a rubber flap and one by a nylon cord) so there is no issue with losing the caps. Most of the barrel is rubberized as well except for the focus knob assembly and where it attaches.

I used it to focus on the tree line behind the house (roughly 30 yards away) and was very pleased with how sharp and clear I was able to get the image. From the front of the house I was able to focus on the stop sign at the end of the street and had no issue with getting fine edge detail even at a distance of roughly a football field. The focus is very smooth and easy to adjust and getting the image in perfect focus is not the least bit difficult.

Though I enjoy cameras and optical equipment and I have learned a good bit about optical equipment I am a far cry from being an expert, so I took this monocular to work and approached two teammates who are very well-versed in optics, photography and astronomy and I asked them to look it over and give me their honest opinion. Both of them examined it and expressed their approval. They both said similar things about it: the image through this monocular is very bright and clear, the focus is very smooth and it seems to be very well made. They both made a comment about the lens and that it was very good due to not having a darkened coating.

One of my teammates told me to try looking at the stars with it. I had not really considered this but knew this would be an excellent test for it so I went outside after dark and pointed it skyward. Though I can definitely see more detail through a dedicated telescope, I was able to make out some of the larger surface detail on the moon including the high point in the middle of a crater. I was hindered by the fact that it is a full moon right now so I will have to try again this weekend during the eclipse. I then picked out a planet and looked at it through the monocular. Though it is a little tough to make out, I know I found Jupiter as I could see three of the moons as bright spots not visible to the naked eye (I have looked at it through a telescope so I recognize it from seeing it already). Finally I discovered a cluster of stars I could not see without magnification. This monocular is certainly not as good as a dedicated telescope but it is sufficient when camping and it eliminates the need to pack a big, bulky telescope unless you want to see more detail.

This is a great tool for use in the field. It has very good range, the image is bright and clear and it even is sufficient for stargazing should you choose to use it for everything on the road. Great product!

Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

I think I'll just do a simple pro and con list for this one.

Pros:

+ It starts up fast when switched on and immediately reconnects to the last Bluetooth device selected.

+ The ability to store multiple device profiles and switch between them with the press of a button is awesome, and it saves a lot of time over having to open the Bluetooth settings on each device to reconnect.

+ And of course it has a 2.4g wireless USB dongle, so you can use it with things that don't have Bluetooth or which require a stronger wireless signal.

+ There are visible-yet-unobtrusive lights on the top that allow you to tell at a glance which device pairing you have selected.

+ The shape of the mouse fits my hand perfectly and is very comfortable.

+ The scroll wheel is easy to grip and roll back and forth. It has a very satisfying sort of "bump" feeling as it rotates from one position to another, whereas some wheels just turn freely, leaving you little control over how much you're actually scrolling. And most importantly, the wheel doesn't rock side-to-side like those ones that supposedly allow you to scroll left and right but never seem to work except by accident when you don't want them to.

+ There's no branding that I can identify on the packaging, the instructions, nor on the mouse itself. I see this as a pro because well, frankly, a lot of these random brand names are weird and bother me (though admittedly, I did once buy a product on Amazon primarily because the brand name was BULLETFACE *cue electric guitar solo*).

+ I really appreciate how every feature on this mouse serves a purpose. There are no dumb shapes or graphics added just to make it look "cool". It's cool enough as it is.

+ It's great that it has a built-in rechargeable battery and a USB-C port on the front so that I can charge it wherever I can charge my phone. But because there's no battery access door, the dongle rests in a recess on the underside of the mouse and is held in by a really strong magnet. That's better than other attachment methods I've seen where the dongle either snaps in with plastic clips or press-fits into a slot, as those will both wear out and fail eventually, where a magnet will not.

Cons:

- The ball feels a bit loose and rattle-y in its socket. It's not an issue when the mouse is on a level surface, but if you're carrying it around or trying to use it on the arm of a sofa, it can wiggle a bit, which feels weird.

- All but the lowest DPI setting is way too fast for anything I can imagine doing, but maybe I'm just not used to it yet. (Update: I guess I wasn't used to it. I've since moved up to the middle DPI setting now that I've gotten better at making fine movements)

- This may not be a con for some people, but the dongle really, really stays put in a USB port, to the point I was afraid I'd need pliers to get it out (though I managed to do so without them).

- Update: I thought of one more con. It's a shame I can't re-bind the little forward and back buttons on the far left to something more useful, like shift or ctrl-z.

Conclusion:

I'm currently very satisfied with my purchase, and I expect to get a lot of use out of this mouse for years to come. The best thing I can do to thank the manufacturer and seller for making a great product at a great price is to leave my honest feedback to help others find the product, so that's exactly what I've done. Oh, and I swyped (typed via path input) this entire review on my phone's on-screen keyboard using the very trackball I'm reviewing, if that gives you an idea of how comfortable and accurate it is to operate.

I have tried to use this lens at f2.8 in low light on a 1.6x crop camera and it just does not look good. Not only is there a large loss of sharpness but for some reason the image becomes more orange on my example. I should mention that with my ebay example the coating on the front element wasn't even, so it's possible that it might be from that.

The lens cap on mine doesn't stay on do to a broken tab, which can be annoying since it's specific to the lens.

I think this lens is a good deal, if it can be had for cheap. I'm not sure I would buy another one if I lost mine at the current prices that this lens goes for though. The primary reason would be because a fisheye lens has limited use do to barrel distortion, I'd rather put that money towards a rectilinear wide angle.

I have been building computer systems and troubleshooting for a long time. I really enjoy taking parts in and out and programming systems to do what I want. I remember looking at a commercial for the new tablets and saying to my family- "What the heck would anyone want one of THOSE things for?" It was not long after they became bored with my insistence that tablets were a total waste that I had my chance to take my first tablet for a test run- the Acer Iconia A1-830.

The Acer was a fantastic little first tablet. It performed as well or better than a few Samsungs and older Apples that we had the chance to put it up against, and for the price, it was a great little tablet. I found some use for it and found myself reaching for the tablet when I didn't want to do work at the computer. It was more portable than a laptop and easier to do quick surfing and simple tasks on, and GAMING.

I thought that all was well until I began to have a few issues with the Acer. It was at that point that I saw a great price on the new Samsung Galaxy Tab S2. I was hooked.

WHAT IS THIS TABLET LIKE?
I plan to write this review to people who are not as interested in the detailed specs of this unit, but instead I will write this for an average user who might not be as technically astute. There are quite a few well done reviews that have lots of specs and details that will satisfy those who really need that information to make decisions.

SCREEN
One of the things that I did not like about the older Samsungs was the size. I preferred the more squared screen of the Acer than the Samsungs I had worked on. My daughter has one and although it seems nice, I just was not keen on the screen. This model has exactly what I wanted to have. The shape makes it easier to work on the web , use as an E reader, and play games. I find it easier to read than more elongated screens.

One of the things that I found to be frustrating is the slick surface of the screen. For web surfing or book reading it is fine, but games can really get frustrating as I find the screen to be very sensitive and it is easy to mess up.

As for the brightness, it is very bright. I have it turned down by about 75% and it is plenty bright enough most of the time. Also, the color contrast is breathtaking. The screen is very sharp and the blacks are BLACK and the colors are very saturated. This thing is eye candy squared! It is hard to look at other screens when I am done using this.

COLOR
This is not really gold in color. I would say it is gold tinged platinum in color. Do not expect a bold gold.

SMOOTHNESS AND UNEVEN EDGES
There are a few things which bug me about this tablet, but not that much. Getting a good case from Fintie took care of it. The button on the bottom of the vertical positioned screen stands out from the unit. That means if you are going to get a keyboard in the case, it could press on the button and cause problems. The Fintie case is raised enough to protect the button.

There is also the camera lens on the back that sticks out quite a bit. Again, the case takes care of that problem. The back itself might be plastic, but it feels like metal and looks like metal so it is not cheap looking.

SPEED AND FUNCTION
WOW is this thing FAST! I have to say that it really has blown me out of the water with the speed and smooth operation of everything I have tried to do. It works smoothly, load up is fast. I know part of that might be due to the inclusion of Lollipop but also the hardware and set up. I have not found it to lag at all. Great performance. I also know that this model is scheduled for the Marshmallow upgrade sometime this year which could change performance to be even better.

I have 32G microSD card in this right now but it is expandable to 128.

BATTERY LIFE
I was very concerned about all of the complaints about battery life. I was so concerned I almost didn't get this tablet. I am SO glad I did, however. I keep location turned off and bluetooth as well unless I am using it. The battery stuns me with how long it has lasted. I loaded that baby up to 100% last night and this morning about 11 AM I began to work intensely on the tablet, trying to back up files from my Acer and transfer them over to the Samsung via bluetooth. That means that the bluetooth was on all day, I was downloading and installing all day long. I have to say that I am shocked. It is about 12 hours later and there is still over 50% battery left. I had to recharge my Acer once during all of this time.

So, compared to what I am used to (which is about 2-4 hours of work on a tablet before recharging, including no location turned on) this tablet is dreamy for me. The battery is way beyond what I am used to with the Acer, so I am very happy.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I will update as I find things to tell you about, but I wanted to start off with the basics as that is what I was looking for when I was trying to decide if I should get this tablet or not. I still do not find tablets to be useful for all of my work, but they are great for smaller web surfing, quick look ups, apps for certain things and of course games and skype. As for the keyboard and typing, it is not really practical at least for me to use this for heavier loads of work- desktop or laptop are best suited for that.

Is it worth the price? At $300 it is a very powerful device with a screen that blows anything else I have seen out of the water. The colors are a feast for the eyes, the clarity is crisp, and the smooth operation is delightful. If you really enjoy having a tablet you can depend on, I would say that this fits the bill.

Could you do with something less expensive? Yes. But you might have more frustration with that lower price tag. The set up of this tablet is easy to work with, great operation and having two windows open at the same time is delightful. I am very happy with this and despite my misgivings after reading so many reviews with disappointment in them I can say at this point, I am very very glad that I went ahead and got it. It is a really great tablet.

I lived and breathed full-sized Kensington trackball mice from about 1987 until my last one stopped functioning and I couldn't find them anymore...probably in the late '90s. Tried some others; all had small, lightweight balls that gave none of the feel and control of Kensinton's...Expert Mouse? Was that what it was called back then too? Because it was the same general design as the current Expert Mouse, but the body was computer-case white.

Anyway, I had several of those (the quality going downhill with each iteration, as I recall) and loved them, and since they disappeared (as far as I could tell), I adapted, first to trackpads, which I've never liked much, and then back to traditional mice which don't give nearly the control of a trackball. Now, at last, it seems Kensington has again begun to produce truly worthwhile trackball mice, and this is one. Oh, it's _so_ good to have one of these again.

I'm doing that thing I hate when other people do it and reviewing the product as soon as I've gotten it up and running, without any kind of experiential history behind my assessment. I'll come back and update this in the future if necessary. But so far: I'm happy, happy, happy to have a real, full-sized Kensington trackball mouse again, with a heavy, substantial ball. There are only two things about this device that I'm not crazy about: In my old Kensington mice, the ball rested on physical rollers and I could give the ball a good spin and it would keep spinning for a second before stopping; it spun much more freely in its cavity than this ball does (so far...maybe that's something that will break in?) [Update: yes, after about three days of use the ball rolls more smoothly and silently than the old one on rollers ever did]. And the other thing is the scrolling mechanism. It's weird. Despite the KensingtonWorks software trying to make us believe otherwise, the "scroll ring" itself actually has nothing to do with scrolling, nor with anything else - the "scroll ring" is not even a control, but just a static piece of chrome trim. What makes the mouse scroll is twisting the ball this way or that from the top, as if it were a knob. At first I thought the "scroll ring" wasn't working because I was trying to use it without touching the ball...which does nothing. And now that I've figured out how scrolling works (you rest your finger on the "scroll ring" and push and pull the side of the ball)...I'm not crazy about it. I'm getting used to it, but it's just a weird way to scroll (I can't for the life of me remember how I used to do it on the Expert Mouse decades ago). It does work though.

(Update on the scrolling: I'm also not crazy about the way the KensingtonWorks software handles the scrolling speed adjustment. When you make the base pointer movement speed faster, the pointer continues to move smoothly, but just faster. When you make the scrolling speed faster though, you lose all smoothness - the software makes the scrolling faster by breaking it into successively larger and more jarring jumps. At the slowest speed, it's pretty smooth; at the highest speeds it's no longer really scrolling, but simply jumping abruptly from one screenful (or page) to the next. Increasing the scrolling speed just increases the size of these jumps, but I find them jarring and annoying starting at the second or third lowest speed setting.)

I also had to figure out how to program one of the buttons as a click lock, since Kensington doesn't call it that anymore, but calls it "left drag", "right drag", and "middle drag" (and I have no idea what the difference is between those three - I just chose "left drag" and it's working fine).

So far, those are my only gripes, all minor. So happy to have one of these things again! =) (Did I mention that?)

Budget-priced earbuds are complicated to review because, in my experience, all $200 earbuds sound significantly better than all $50 earbuds, but there is still a lot of demand for value-priced "good enough" products. I do own a couple of $200 earbuds and they do sound noticeably richer and clearer than these $40 earbuds. However, when I'm out jogging or traveling (eg airplane or train) or listening to voice podcasts, having the absolute best sound quality isn't really important to me. In those situations, features are more important to me, like active noise cancellation, equalization, good volume, good battery life, and easy access to the features. I'd rather use cheap earbuds that I don't mind losing somewhere along the way.

These earbuds have average quality sound for the $40 price. Where these Donner earbuds beat the competition is the features. I've never owned $40 earbuds with app control before. The user manual has a QR code to let you download the app. The QR code did not work, but I did find the "Donner Control" app in the Google Play app store and the app works fine on my Android phone. The app lets me pick from pre-programmed equalization settings or design my own. Adjusting the equalization for different types of music makes a significant difference in audio clarity. The app also lets me choose from 3 active noise cancellation modes. These features don't work as well as in $200 earbuds, but these are $40 earbuds and most $40 earbuds don't have any of these features or any app at all. You can control some of these features with the confusing set of triple-tap commands on the earbuds, but I can never remember those and would rather just tap the picture in the app.

The app also lets you download firmware updates from Donner. None was available when I checked, but this could be a great way for them to refine the features of the earbuds or even add new features. They ask you to give them your email address and create an account when you open the app, but I did not and the core features of the app still work OK.

Battery life for these earbuds is good for this price range (6 to 8 hours, depending on whether or not you use ANC). As with most budget-priced wireless earbuds, maximum volume is OK but not great. Bass is above average for the $40 price. Static noise is very low. The Bluetooth connection has been very stable for me, even when I'm 30 feet away from my phone or in a different room in the house.

I can't give these earbuds 5 stars because I can easily buy better sound quality with more money, but these are solid 4 stars for value at the current $40 price.

Okay, For a pair of headphones that cost me less than 10 bucks, I didn't expect anything that great anyways. You get what you pay for, they're not bad, but they're not that great either. This is why: Sound quality is pretty weak, it's not just flat, but a bit tinny, on the trebles and the bass is pretty weak. The fit is unergonomic, it's just this generic round shape that runs a little big, so if you have small ears, the fit will be awkward. I've only had it for a week so, so far there are no problems with the durability. I like how the plug end is flexible, so I know int he future the wires aren't gonna fray and break. The cable is pretty flexible too, I don;t anticipate any crimping. The plastic housing on the wires and ear pieces themselves are alright for the price. I bought these cause I wanted some cheap disposable in ears for cycling. I can still hear what's going on outside while wearing these. They're a bit quieter than my regular in ear headphones. The bottom line is, if you want cheap earphones that work decently, these are fine. If you're used to better sound quality, these may jar you.
I also want to compare these to the earbuds that came with my zune player. The Zune earbuds are much better in sound quality and fit. After using it for two years, they broke so I bought these as a replacement. For around the same price, under 10 dollars, the zune ones are better.
